So Muʿammar includes generated actions within voluntary action, unlike al-ʿAllāf and al-Iskāfī.
Thumāma ibn Ashras al-Numayrī, a Baghdad Muʿtazilite who died in 213 AH/828 CE, also distinguishes between voluntary acts and generated acts. But he argues that “generated acts have no agent.”

Al-Shahrastānī explains why. Thumāma could not attribute a generated act to the person who caused it, because that would sometimes force him to attribute an action to someone who was already dead. A person might perform the original act, die, and only afterward would the generated effect occur.
Nor could Thumāma attribute the generated act to God, because that could mean attributing an evil act to God, which he considered impossible.
So, al-Shahrastānī says, Thumāma was left without an answer and concluded: “Generated acts are acts with no agent.”

Al-Jāḥiẓ, by contrast, followed the Muʿtazilite position associated with al-ʿAllāf. He distinguished voluntary action from necessary natural action by saying that a human being has no act other than the will, while all other accidents are actions that bodies produce according to their own nature.
In other words, these are actions governed by necessary, objective laws of nature.

Al-Aswārī, one of al-Naẓẓām’s followers, held a view that was not fundamentally different from that of al-ʿAllāf and others who followed the same path. But al-Aswārī used a different way of defining voluntary action—that is, human action.

While discussing the limits of God’s power, he says that God cannot be described as having the power to do something He knows He will not do, or something He has said He will not do. A human being, however, can have such power, because “the servant’s power extends to both opposites.”
What he means is that a person’s knowledge does not remove freedom of choice.
Before choosing between two opposite actions, a person is capable of doing either one. This remains true whether the person knows that he will do something or knows that he will not do it.
For the followers of al-Naẓẓām, this is another expression of human freedom in action.

When it comes to nature, however, they accept the Muʿtazilite idea that natural events are governed by objective and necessary laws, even though al-Naẓẓām ultimately traces those laws back to a divine source.
Al-Shahrastānī reports a statement transmitted by al-Kaʿbī—Abū al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad al-Balkhī, a Baghdad Muʿtazilite who died in 319 AH/931 CE—in which al-Naẓẓām says:

“Every act that goes beyond the limit of human capacity”—meaning human power and will—“is an act of God through the necessity built into creation. God gave the stone a nature and created it in such a way that, when someone pushes it and the force of the push has run its course, it naturally returns to its place.”
This clearly shows al-Naẓẓām recognizing that natural events take place according to general and necessary laws, such as the law of causation and the law of motion.
The Muʿtazilites believed that human beings are unique among living beings because they can freely choose their actions. They also believed that reason is what gives human beings this freedom.

It was therefore natural for them to ask how people acquire knowledge, what part reason plays in the process, how far reason can reach, what different kinds of knowledge exist, what means we have for acquiring each kind, how each kind is acquired, and how much value we should place on knowledge gained in one way rather than another.
These questions form part of the foundations of the Muʿtazilite doctrine of justice.
The wider and deeper the powers of human reason are, and the more knowledge reason can attain, the stronger the Muʿtazilite case for their doctrine of justice becomes.
So how did they approach the problem?
To give the question reasonably full treatment, we can follow the traditional division of knowledge into two main kinds: sensory knowledge and rational knowledge.
This division remains logically useful, and it also matches the way the Muʿtazilites themselves approached the subject.

The Muʿtazilite discussion of sensory knowledge is closely connected to their extensive debates about the human soul or spirit: its relationship with the body, its relationship with the five sense organs, the relationship of those senses to one another, and the part each sense plays in knowledge.
Their accounts of the soul or spirit differed greatly. As a result, they also disagreed about the part it plays in sensation and perception—that is, in knowledge.
The first name that stands out here is Ibrāhīm al-Naẓẓām, because he discussed the subject at great length.

We have already seen that al-Naẓẓām identifies the human being with the soul or spirit. He says that the soul penetrates the body and is interwoven with it so completely that, as he puts it, “every part of this is with every part of that.” In other words, every part of the soul is present with every part of the body.
But he also regards the body as an impediment to the soul.
Al-Ashʿarī reports a statement that Zurqān attributed to al-Naẓẓām: “The soul is what senses and perceives. It is one single thing, and it is neither light nor darkness.”

If this statement really belongs to al-Naẓẓām, we can draw an important conclusion from it. The soul would then be the source of every power of sensation and perception, including the power to perceive the outside world through the senses.
But the surviving reports about al-Naẓẓām’s view of the relationship between soul and body are themselves inconsistent.
In one place, al-Ashʿarī reports him as saying that “the spirit is the body and is the soul.”
Al-Shahrastānī, however, reports him as saying:
“The human being in the true sense is the soul and the spirit, while the body is its instrument and its mould.”

Al-Shahrastānī adds that al-Naẓẓām leaned toward the view of the natural philosophers, according to which the soul is a subtle body interwoven with the physical body. It enters into the body in every part, “as water enters the rose, oil enters sesame, and fat enters milk.”

Looking across the different statements attributed to al-Naẓẓām in our sources, it seems that his basic position is still a dualism between soul and body, despite the extremely close interpenetration he describes between them.
What matters for us here, however, is his view of where sensory perception comes from.

From what we have already seen, we can conclude that al-Naẓẓām describes the soul as “what senses and perceives.” If the soul is different from the body, and if the soul is what senses and perceives, then it follows that he does not recognize the bodily senses as independent powers of perception.
On this view, it is the soul—not the body—that perceives sensible things through the openings we call the ear, mouth, nose, and eye.

A person does not possess a faculty of hearing separate from himself, or a faculty of sight separate from himself. Rather, the person hears through the self and may become deaf because of some defect affecting him. Likewise, he sees through the self and may become blind because of some defect affecting him.
So according to this account, a person does not have a separate faculty of hearing apart from the soul, which for al-Naẓẓām is the person himself. The same is true of sight.

A human being hears and sees through the soul alone. If he becomes deaf or blind, the deafness or blindness affects the soul itself because of some defect that has affected the human being—that is, the soul.
The physical organs that we normally call the five sense organs are therefore only openings or channels. The soul uses them as routes through which it reaches the things it perceives.

The soul “leaps” through the opening of the eye toward the object being seen, enters into contact with it, and comes alongside it. In the same way, it leaps through the opening of the ear, meets the sound and joins with it, and thus hears it. The same applies to smell and taste.
Sensory knowledge, then, is for al-Naẓẓām an internal function of the soul. It is not produced by the external bodily organs that we normally call the five senses.
This also helps explain his view that the senses are not different powers in themselves. They all operate through a single power.

Al-Jāḥiẓ describes the view in these words: the senses “belong to one kind. The sense of sight is of the same kind as the sense of hearing and all the other senses. The difference lies only in the kind of thing perceived and in the locations of the senses. There is no other difference between them.”
If the soul itself is the source of all sensory knowledge, then it follows naturally that the senses belong to one kind, because the soul itself is one.
But how can this explain the obvious differences between our senses? Hearing is clearly different from sight, and both are different from smell, taste, and touch.
The statement from al-Jāḥiẓ points toward an answer.
What differs, on this view, is not the senses themselves. The difference comes from two things.
The first is the kind of object being perceived.
The second is the location through which the soul perceives things in the outside world.
Al-Naẓẓām himself explains what he means by the obstacles involved. He says:

“What prevents hearing from perceiving color is something mixed with it, an obstruction of the same kind as darkness, which prevents the perception of color but not the perception of sound. What prevents sight from perceiving sounds is something mixed with it of the same kind as glass, which prevents the perception of sound but not the perception of color.”
Al-Naẓẓām used this same idea to explain the different obstacles and obstructions affecting the various senses and the openings through which they operate.
So hearing, sight, and the other senses all come from one power: the power of the soul or spirit.
By its own nature, this power would be capable of hearing color or seeing sound. What prevents it from doing so are obstacles that do not belong to the soul’s own nature.
The sensory faculty as a whole is surrounded by different kinds of obstacles. Each sense is affected by a different kind of obstacle.

Things in the outside world also have many different qualities, and these qualities affect the senses in different ways. A sense therefore responds only to those qualities that are not blocked by the particular obstacles affecting it.
What, then, can we conclude from al-Naẓẓām’s explanation of how we sense the external world—in other words, of sensory knowledge?

It seems to us that his account ultimately turns what we call sensory knowledge into a kind of rational perception. The main difference is simply that sensory knowledge deals with the qualities of things in the outside world.
The bodily senses themselves are little more than channels through which those qualities pass. Through them, the sensible object affects the perceiver, who is the soul—that is, the human being.
All of this leads us to accept the view that al-Naẓẓām and al-Jāḥiẓ were influenced here by Aristotle’s account of sensory knowledge.

Aristotle says that the soul perceives through these openings and channels. They become different senses—one hearing, another sight, another smell—because of the different obstacles mixed with them. But the underlying faculty that senses does not itself differ. If it did, the different senses would obstruct and destroy one another, just as different and opposing things do.

Al-Naẓẓām’s overall position clearly rests on his belief that the human being is the soul or spirit, while the body is only a temporary dwelling or mould for it. This is why he assigns all the functions of sensation and perception directly to the soul.
Yet al-Naẓẓām also made another attempt to explain sensory knowledge, this time by looking at the interaction between the thing perceived and the faculty that perceives it.

“Sight perceives colors because color is transmitted from the perceived object. If there were more of it, its effect would be stronger; and if it became excessive, we would no longer perceive any color at all.”
This does not overturn his earlier position about the source of sensation in the perceiver.
We can say instead that his earlier account explained sensory knowledge from one side of the process: the perceiver, meaning the soul.
This later statement approaches the same process from the other side: the object being perceived.
His earlier treatment had a clearly metaphysical character. Here, however, we see a more physical approach with a significant materialist content.
Al-Naẓẓām is now trying to identify what determines whether sensible things affect our senses and how strongly they do so. To explain this, he turns to physical features of the things themselves.

He believes that the amount of color present in visible things—whether there is little or much of it—determines the strength of its effect on the senses. The same principle applies to sound, smell, taste, and the other things perceived by the different senses.
We should connect this view of the “amount” of color, sound, smell, and taste with al-Naẓẓām’s theory of accidents.
He is known for denying the existence of accidents in general. In his view, the only true accident is motion.

What other thinkers call accidents are, for al-Naẓẓām, actually very fine bodies emitted by natural things. He regards “colors, tastes, smells, sounds, pains, heat, cold, moisture, and dryness as subtle bodies.”

This is why al-Ashʿarī says that, according to al-Naẓẓām, “nothing is seen except a body, and nothing is heard except a body, because sounds are bodies for him. Likewise, nothing is tasted, smelled, or touched except a body.”
Al-Shahrastānī gives a useful example of this part of al-Naẓẓām’s theory:

“Al-Naẓẓām held that speech is a subtle body emitted by the speaker. It strikes the particles of air, causing the air to move in waves and take on its form. It then strikes the nerve spread through the ear, which takes on the same form. From there it reaches the imagination and is presented to rational thought, which understands it.”
We can apply the same reasoning to color, taste, and smell.
It is clear that al-Naẓẓām’s conclusions here are not very far from some of the results reached by modern experimental science in the physical sciences.
But the same example also reveals another side of his theory of knowledge.

It gives us a clear picture of how he imagines the stages of knowledge unfolding one after another: beginning with the direct effect of sensible things on the nerves of the senses and ending with the final stage, where those effects enter the realm of rational knowledge.
From this we can conclude that the direct object of sensory knowledge is the external world: a world made up of natural bodies with a real, objective existence.
That same external world also becomes, in the end, the indirect object of rational knowledge.
But does al-Naẓẓām believe that the external world is the only object of rational knowledge?
We will answer that question when we turn to Muʿtazilite views on rational knowledge.
For now, what we can conclude is that sensory knowledge can give us knowledge that the thinking mind can then use.
Our final conclusion from al-Naẓẓām’s views on sensory knowledge is that, taken as a whole, they contain two almost opposing sides.

One is purely metaphysical. This appears in his view of the powers of sensory perception. He locates these powers entirely in the soul or spirit, while separating soul from body and treating their relationship in dualistic terms.
The other side is materialist. We see it in his account of the nature of sensible things and the way they affect the senses.
If we use the language of Marxist philosophical writing, we can say that al-Naẓẓām’s theory of sensory knowledge as a whole represents one historical form of “objective idealism.”
The same description may also apply to many other Muʿtazilite ideas and theories.

This becomes clearer when we remember that the great majority of Muʿtazilite thinkers begin from the view that the body is an objective natural reality. They also accept that bodies physically affect the sources of sensation and the centers of perception in human beings, even though their understanding of those sources and centers is usually metaphysical.
